text: We say we found Jesus. The truth is, someone brought us to Him.
explanation:
Under the law, a leper was cut off from everyone: he couldn't hold his baby or embrace his wife. Yet Leviticus says that on the day of his cleansing, "he shall be brought to the priest." Someone cared enough to bring him. That unnamed helper is a picture of the Holy Spirit.

Man could never reach God by his works, so God reached down to man. If you know Jesus today, it isn't because you were clever enough to find Him. The Spirit drew you, brought you, and placed you before your great High Priest.

text: The older brother never left home, yet he was far from his father. Everything was his, and he never knew it.
explanation:
When the prodigal came home to music and dancing, the older brother had to ask what it meant. He refused to go in, and when his father came out to plead with him he said, "All these years I have served you and never transgressed your commandment, yet you never gave me even a young goat."

The father replied tenderly, "Child, you are always with me, and all that I have is yours." He could have had the fatted calf any day. It's possible to be close to God in position, through Jesus, and still distant in heart because of wrong believing. God is generous; we only receive what we believe.

text: In 3 John 2, "prosper" is passive but "be in health" isn't. Health is something you actively reach out and take hold of.
explanation:
"Beloved, I pray that you may prosper in all things and be in health, just as your soul prospers." In Greek, "prosper" is a present passive: something you receive. "Be in health" is not passive. That may be why some people prosper easily but struggle physically: they wait for healing to drop on them.

So take part actively: receive the Lord's Supper, and declare "by His stripes I am healed." And notice what surrounds the verse: "walk in the truth" appears again and again. Your soul prospers as you walk in the truth of the gospel of grace, and blessing follows from there.

text: You don't hope you're forgiven. You have it, according to the riches of His grace.
explanation:
"In Him we have redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of His grace." "Have" is present and active in Greek, and the word also means to hold fast and possess. Hold on to it, because people will try to talk you out of it.

The first-century church was marked by bold, certain faith: "through this Man is preached to you the forgiveness of sins." Some today call that certainty presumption and doubt humility. But God didn't forgive cheaply; redemption was paid with Jesus' blood. Lay out all of God's riches and you still won't reach the end of how forgiven you are.

text: The servant forgiven millions grabbed a man who owed him a few thousand. He never really heard that he'd been forgiven.
explanation:
Facing ruin, the servant begged, "Be patient with me, and I will pay you all." He couldn't have repaid it in a lifetime, but he still believed he could. The king had compassion and cancelled the entire debt. Yet straight away the man went out and seized a fellow servant by the throat over a small sum.

He walked away still thinking in terms of paying, not in terms of being forgiven. Some believers are forgiven but never enjoy it, so they have nothing to give others. When you really take in how much you've been released from, you'll want to release everyone around you.

text: Before the cross: forgive, so you'll be forgiven. After the cross: forgive, because you have been.
explanation:
Jesus told His Jewish hearers, before His death, "If you do not forgive men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses." After the cross, Paul writes to believers: "forgiving one another, even as God in Christ forgave you": a completed, once-for-all act.

Threatening people with "forgive or you won't be forgiven" gives them no power to do it. The only firm foundation for forgiving others is knowing how completely you've been forgiven. Bitterness loosens its grip when you're overwhelmed by grace.

text: Seventy times seven doesn't mean 490. It means stop counting.
explanation:
Peter thought he was being generous: "Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Up to seven times?" Jesus answered, "Not seven times, but seventy times seven." Seven is the number of perfection, so this is perfection multiplied: without limit.

Any marriage, family or friendship will need this. There will always be something new to forgive. Couples who say "we'll never need to forgive each other" haven't been married long. Draw from the forgiveness you've received, and keep no record.
